roles.narrative:
**BACKGROUND**

You are a freelance content writer working from home, but you want to move to a rented office space. Although you can't afford to do it on your own, you found two other professionals in a similar situation who might want to share: an academic coordinator and a workshop facilitator.

The three of you must decide how the space will operate, such as how to set up the office and how the office is used after work hours. All three of you use workspaces in different ways. Your goal here is to agree on a sharing situation that will help get you out of the house while meeting your budgetary and functional needs.

In a few minutes, all three of you will join a video call to discuss each of these possible office features. Some features keep costs low, some features support focused quiet work, and others support things like meetings and group activity. Each feature can either be **INCLUDED** or **EXCLUDED** from the final office agreement.

Your office mates benefit from different features.

- The academic coordinator often needs space for meetings, planning sessions, and quick check-ins. Their work runs on a tight budget, so they care about keeping costs low.
- The workshop facilitator runs coaching sessions and professional development workshops for paying clients. They care about a space that feels professional and focused, but also can be arranged for events and group sessions.

As you read your role materials below, try to “get into character.” A negotiation activity is a bit like acting: think about what your character wants, how they see the shared office, and how you would advocate for your preferred features. The points you earn will become your Prolific bonus, so prepare to negotiate for the best possible outcome!

**About You**

As a freelance content writer, you spend your days writing articles, editing client drafts, and turning ideas into written materials. Your work is mentally demanding and requires long stretches of concentration, especially when you are trying to meet a deadline.

You don’t want to work from home all the time. You like being around other working people, having short breaks, and feeling like your workday has some structure.

At the same time, you don’t want the office to turn into a meeting room or event venue where people are constantly talking, moving furniture, bringing visitors, or otherwise making noise. You don’t need meeting or event spaces. Your income can vary month to month, so affordability is important.

You don’t want to go back to expensive cafés just to get out of the house, so you’re hopeful this works out. But you won't agree to anything that is a net negative for you.

Your priorities are: **Cost Efficiency** and having **Focused Work Spaces**.

- You want the group to purchase secondhand furniture, use self-managed cleaning, and choose the smaller office space.
- These choices keep the office realistic for three people paying out of pocket, and a shared office doesn’t need to feel fancy or oversized to work well.
- To support focus and minimize distractions, you want strict visitor time windows and to turn the kitchen into a private call room outside lunch hours.
- You want strict quiet time in the mornings, so everyone can get their hardest tasks done with focus at the start of the day.
- You are against spending money and space on a large meeting table at the center of the office, allowing evening events in the office, and adding a divider for a guest meeting room.
- Evening events, meeting tables, and meeting rooms bring in noise and reduce usable working space. People should take their in-person meetings elsewhere, right?

Your preferences across each issue are summarized below. Higher points mean you like that option more, and the total points you receive if your group reaches an agreement will determine the amount of bonus money you earn from Prolific, in addition to the fixed payment.
roles.BATNA: If you can’t reach agreement, your fallback plan is to keep working from home, worth 0 points.

**About You**

As an academic coordinator, you spend a good chunk of your day booking sessions for freelance tutors, speaking with families, and advising students on study plans and college admissions. A lot happens by email, but you still need to be available throughout the day for phone calls, and to occasionally meet local clients in person.

You also organize small events for tutors and students. Sometimes that means after-work socials where tutors exchange tips. Sometimes it means practical matching sessions where students meet possible tutors. You host these work meetings at home or in public places. However, you live with roommates to save costs, and so you want to avoid bringing clients there even if they don’t seem to mind. You don’t want to work from home all the time either. You get very distracted there. You want a real place where you can meet office mates, hold small meetings, and stay away from the distractions of home.

At the same time, you’re not trying to create a noisy event venue. You just need the office to be comfortable for everyday admin work, occasional group sessions, and people coming in and out for scheduled meetings. Your work runs on a very tight budget, so the space needs to stay affordable while still supporting meetings and shared work.

Your priorities are: **Cost Efficiency** and having adequate **Events and Meeting Space**.

- You want the group to purchase secondhand furniture, use self-managed cleaning, and choose the smaller office space.
- These choices keep the office realistic for three people paying out of pocket, while still leaving money and space for features that make the office useful for meetings and shared work.
- To support meetings and shared work, you want to allow evening events, add a divider for a guest meeting room, and place a large meeting table at the center of the office.
- These features help you meet families, students, tutors, and clients in a setting that feels more appropriate than your home or a café.
- You are against strict visitor time windows, using the kitchen as a private call room, and strict morning quiet time.
- Visitor windows are hard for you because students, families, and tutors often have limited availability, so you cannot always fit meetings into narrow time slots.
- The kitchen also needs to remain a casual hospitality space where you can offer guests tea, coffee, or a snack, even outside lunch hours.
- Strict morning quiet time is difficult because your work depends on coordination, quick calls, and short conversations throughout the day. Why share an office if you can’t talk through plans or handle quick coordination when the day starts, right?

**About You**

You are a workshop facilitator. You spend most of your day doing admin work, preparing slides, designing materials, and planning professional development or team-building workshops. Sometimes you meet clients virtually or in person during the day. Sometimes you run small workshops for companies during work hours. But a lot of your work happens on nights and weekends, when professionals are free to attend sessions after work.

A lot of your work depends on the room feeling calm and credible, but also flexible enough for discussion, activities, and people moving around. You don’t want to work from home all the time. You like having a proper space where you can socialize with co-workers, prepare materials, take client calls, and welcome workshop clients into a room that feels like it was meant for this kind of work.

At the same time, you’re not trying to create an overly expensive showpiece. Budget still matters. It’s just not the only thing that matters. You believe that having a productive space where you can do focused work, take Zoom calls, and show clients around is part of how you make more money. Cutting costs too far can backfire if it makes the office feel cramped, improvised, or hard to use. You want the office to support quiet client conversations, small group sessions, and focused work during the day, while still being useful for events and workshops after typical working hours.

Your priorities are: having **Focused Work Spaces** and adequate **Events and Meeting Space**.

- You want strict visitor time windows, to use the kitchen as a private call room, and to have strict morning quiet time.
- These choices make the office calmer and more predictable during the day, especially when people need to focus, prepare materials, or take client calls.
- You are not against guests. You just want guests to come during agreed windows, so everyone knows when the office will be more social and when it will be quieter.
- To support workshops and client-facing work, you want to allow evening events, add a divider for a guest meeting room, and place a large meeting table at the center of the office.
- These features make the office useful for paid workshops, group exercises, client conversations, and professional events after typical working hours.
- You are against secondhand furniture, choosing the smaller office space, and self-managed cleaning.
- These may save money, but they can make the office feel less polished, cramped, or harder to maintain when guests and clients come in.
- Self-managed cleaning is especially risky because it can create unnecessary conflict when people have guests, clients, or workshop participants coming over. Why rent office space if it cannot support professional sessions beyond ordinary desk work, right?

tips:
Important Task and Payment Instructions

  • What determines how much I earn? The points table shows your preferences. Points earned from any agreement become your bonus on Prolific. No agreement means no bonus.
  • How can we reach an agreement? All three people must accept the same final proposal. This proposal must be submitted officially in the system, like in the demo. A verbal agreement is not enough! You may need to submit and vote on multiple proposals to reach agreement.
  • What happens if we don’t reach an agreement? If your group does not reach an agreement, everyone will keep working from home. This outcome is worth 0 points.
  • What if my group is incomplete? If someone quits or stops responding, you may end the game early by clicking the quit button.
  • How should I prepare? Get into character! Think about how you would introduce yourself, what you want, and how you might advocate for your best outcome.
